For a nonzero linear projection, preimages in the convex body of compact subsets of the line are compact, and the Minkowski combination of two preimages lies in the preimage of the corresponding combination. Brunn–Minkowski gives measure parameter 1/d. The pushforward has no atoms because the level sets have d-dimensional volume zero, and its centered first moment is zero. In d=1 the centered uniform interval is symmetric and continuous, including both support endpoints.

Checked Fradelizi–Guédon, DCG 31 (2004), pp. 329–330, §2 and Theorems 1–2, DOI 10.1007/s00454-003-2868-y, against the author-hosted published article at https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/fradelizi.matthieu/pdf/localizationDCG.pdf. A compact interval, a continuous test function x, and a bounded affine functional on all interval probabilities satisfy the theorem. Both closed-ray mass functions are weakly upper semicontinuous by Portmanteau. The mean constraint is a single inequality and the original law lies in the admissible set. The parameter 1/d is in (0,1/2], including d=2. The maximizing Dirac lies at x≥0 and contributes at most one for s>0, including x=s. The binomial expansion gives (1+1/d)^d≥2, so this value is at most 2−2γ_d. The non-Dirac maximizing segment has mean zero. On a one-dimensional support the theorem's measure parameter σ corresponds to the density-root exponent σ/(1−σ), giving power d−1. Testing all centered affine-power segment probabilities covers the extremizers satisfying the theorem's extra one-sided integral condition.

For a strictly increasing affine root ℓ on [a,b], normalize by t=ℓ(x)/ℓ(b), with r=ℓ(a)/ℓ(b) in [0,1). In the centered original variable the shift becomes h=s ℓ′/ℓ(b). The endpoint lemma implies 1−m≤m−r and m<1. On 0≤h≤1−m, H′(h)=f(m+h)−f(m−h)≥0 almost everywhere. From 1−m to m−r, the upper CDF is one and the lower CDF is nonincreasing. From m−r onward H=1. Continuity treats r=0, both clipping thresholds and h=0. Therefore the maximum is 1+G(2m−1) and the minimum is min{2G(m),1}.

For the decreasing density, nonatomic reflection gives 2−H(h) exactly, including support endpoints. The convex frustum tL, r≤t≤1, has first-coordinate marginal f and centroid coordinate m. It is compact and convex, including the cone vertex when r=0, and has positive d-volume because L is a (d−1)-dimensional convex body and r<1. The accepted full-volume depth bound gives G(m)≥γ_d, and 1≥2γ_d, so the reflected objective is at most 2−2γ_d. The remaining constant affine root gives paired CDF identically one.

For the original atomless law the closed CDF at each threshold and the closed upper tail there add to one. This converts the upper bound to the claimed lower bound. Letting s decrease to zero gives 2F(0) by continuity. For a simplex with tL sections on [0,1], the CDF is t^d and the mean is d/(d+1). In direction −e₁ the tail at zero equals that CDF at the mean, exactly γ_d. The same equality holds in d=1 for an interval. As a separate exact endpoint calibration, the increasing triangular law has G(2m−1)=1/9 at r=0, giving paired upper tails 8/9 at shift 1/3.

Independence makes the conditional halfspace probability F(−u·Y). Symmetry of u·Y replaces its expectation by the average of the two signs, so atoms of the noise, including at zero, are allowed. This uses no first moment for the halfspace bound. A finite first moment yields E[Y]=0 by symmetry, so the convolution mean is g. Zero noise in the simplex direction attains γ_d.

The finite integer set P∩Z^n is nonempty because its center j belongs to P and is integral. The product has the same fiber volume at every site, so normalized mixed mass is exactly the independent joint uniform law. The map I↦2j−I preserves the sites and their weights. For a normal (b,u) with u≠0 apply the scalar pairing to the independent shift b·(I−j), with no need for a vector-noise representation. For u=0 the probability is (1+Pr[b·(I−j)=0])/2. Every containing closed halfspace contains a parallel halfspace whose boundary contains (j,g).

dependencies.mapping: The increasing affine root gives precisely the lemma's d≥2, 0≤r<1, normalized t^{d−1} law with the same G and m. The lemma is used for r≤2m−1<1, which orders the clipping thresholds, and for the upper bound G(2m−1)≤1−2γ_d on the CDF at the first clipping threshold.

Use the right inclusion of the metronoid lemma on the frustum, with its volume a>0, metronoid mass a, and admissible density f≡1. Its volume centroid belongs to the full-volume metronoid. The closed halfspace t≤m contains that centroid on its boundary. Dividing the resulting γ_d a lower bound by a proves G(m)≥γ_d. The metronoid lemma's other inclusion is unused.

overlap.comparison: The full-volume metronoid specialization is exactly the convex-body zero-shift bound. It supplies a premise for the new proof and does not control positive shifts.

The symmetric-kernel bound gives at least one half at (j,g) when K is itself centrally symmetric. With asymmetric K its product specialization depends on vol_d(K∩(2g−K))/(2 vol_d K), so it does not supply the candidate's γ_d depth.

Lattice fiber-volume symmetry applies to the product, but gives a selected point in the central fiber with normalized depth at least 1/(80n). The candidate fixes the volume centroid of that fiber and gives γ_d independent of n.
Constant volume roots make the hypothesis hold with ε=0 and give the weaker normalized depth γ_d/2^n at a selected actual-fiber centroid. The result does not control every paired scalar cut.

Uses the same localization theorem for centered log-concave laws with parameter zero, but bounds F(0)+2F(h)+F(2h)−P(−2h) by 1/3. That expression and bound do not give the two-shift estimate with 2γ_d.

A convolution of scaled independent uniforms yields a 1/e union bound and a mixed-mass lower bound weighted by the minimum retained coefficient. It does not give γ_d for arbitrary independent symmetric additive noise or for the mixed-product centroid.
